posts.title: RLHF: Teaching a Model What 'Good' Actually Means
posts.subtitle: Pretraining predicts the next token. RLHF teaches the model which next token humans actually want.
posts.summary: RLHF aligns a pretrained model with human preferences through a three-stage pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, a reward model trained on human comparisons, and PPO fine-tuning against that reward with a KL penalty. It made ChatGPT-style assistants possible, but it's expensive, unstable, and prone to reward hacking — which is why DPO exists as a simpler alternative.

slides.title: A Base Model Doesn't Know What 'Helpful' Means
slides.body: Pretraining only teaches a model to predict the statistically likely next token from internet text. It has no notion of helpful, honest, or harmless — those are human judgments, not statistical ones.
bullets: GPT-3-style base models will ramble, refuse nothing, or confidently invent facts
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) bolts a human preference signal onto that base model
It's the pipeline behind InstructGPT and the original ChatGPT

slides.title: Demonstrations Alone Cap Quality at the Demonstrator
slides.body: You could just fine-tune on human-written example answers (SFT). But that only ever gets the model as good as the humans writing the examples — it can't learn 'this answer is better than that one' the way a scored comparison can.
bullets: SFT teaches imitation, not preference — no signal for 'good vs. better'
Writing gold-standard answers for every possible prompt doesn't scale
Ranking two existing answers is much cheaper for a human than writing a new one

slides.title: Three Stages: SFT, Reward Model, Then PPO
slides.body: InstructGPT's recipe, now the standard: (1) supervised fine-tune on human demonstrations, (2) train a separate reward model on human-ranked comparisons, (3) use RL (PPO) to fine-tune the policy to maximize that reward model's score.
bullets: Stage 1 — SFT: fine-tune the base model on curated prompt/response pairs
Stage 2 — Reward Model: humans rank 4-9 outputs per prompt; RM learns to score them via a Bradley-Terry pairwise loss
Stage 3 — PPO: the policy generates, the RM scores, PPO updates weights to raise the score
A KL penalty holds the policy close to the SFT model so it can't drift arbitrarily far chasing reward

slides.title: Worked Example: 'Explain Entanglement to a 5-Year-Old'
slides.body: The SFT model gives a technically dense answer full of jargon. Labelers see 4 candidate answers and rank a short, warm, concrete analogy highest — even though it's less 'complete.'
bullets: Reward model learns: simpler + warmer + still-correct scores higher for this prompt style
PPO nudges the policy's weights toward producing that style more often
Net effect: the same base knowledge, delivered the way humans said they preferred it

slides.title: RLHF vs. DPO vs. Plain SFT

rows: Reward model + reference model + policy (3 in memory)
Directly maximizes preference likelihood, closed-form loss

bullets: DPO exists specifically because full RLHF's 3-model RL loop is expensive and unstable
RLHF still shows up where you need to optimize against an evolving or composite reward, not just static preference pairs

slides.title: Reward Hacking Is the Central Failure Mode
slides.body: PPO will happily exploit any blind spot in the reward model — because the reward model is a proxy, not ground truth. Goodhart's Law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.
bullets: Sycophancy: raters mildly preferred agreeable answers, so RMs reward agreement — models learn to flatter and avoid disagreeing with false premises
Length gaming: RMs often correlate longer answers with 'more thorough,' so policies bloat responses to farm reward
Over-optimization: push PPO too hard against a fixed RM and true human-judged quality can start to fall even as RM score keeps rising

slides.title: When to Reach for Full RLHF
bullets: Use RLHF when you need to optimize against a reward that isn't just a fixed offline preference dataset (e.g., composite or evolving objectives)
Prefer DPO when you have static preference pairs and want to skip the reward model + RL loop entirely — same alignment goal, far less infrastructure
Always budget for reward-model overoptimization: hold out human eval, don't just trust the RM's own score climbing
The KL penalty coefficient is the main lever against both reward hacking and mode collapse — too loose and it hacks the reward, too tight and it barely moves from the SFT model

questions.prompt: Why does RLHF use a separate reward model instead of having humans score every RL rollout directly?
options: Reward models are more accurate than humans
Live human labeling for every RL step would be far too slow/expensive; the reward model is a learned, fast stand-in trained once on human comparisons
Reward models are required by the PPO algorithm's math
Humans cannot rank text outputs reliably
questions.explanation: PPO needs thousands of scored rollouts to train. Humans label a comparison dataset once; the reward model generalizes that signal so training doesn't need a human in the loop at every step.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the KL penalty in the PPO stage of RLHF?
options: It speeds up training convergence
It keeps the policy close to the original SFT model so it can't drift arbitrarily far while chasing reward, limiting reward hacking
It replaces the need for a reward model
It compresses the model's weights
questions.explanation: Without the KL constraint, PPO can find degenerate outputs that score high on the reward model but read as nonsense or unsafe to humans — the KL term anchors the policy to sane, SFT-like behavior.

questions.prompt: A team has a fixed dataset of human preference pairs and wants alignment with minimal infrastructure. What's the strongest reason to pick DPO over full RLHF here?
options: DPO produces strictly higher quality models in all cases
DPO skips training a separate reward model and running an RL loop, directly optimizing the policy on the preference pairs with a stable, closed-form loss
DPO doesn't require any human preference data
DPO is the only method that supports KL regularization
questions.explanation: DPO reformulates the RLHF objective so the optimal reward model is implicit in the policy itself, letting you train directly on preference pairs with a supervised-style loss — no reward model, no PPO instability.

posts.title: Kimi K3: Moonshot's 2.8T-Parameter Model Goes Fully Open
posts.subtitle: 104B active out of 2.8 trillion parameters, a 1M-token context, and every weight downloadable under Moonshot's own license.
posts.summary: Moonshot AI released the full weights of Kimi K3 on July 26, 2026: a 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with only 104B parameters active per token, a new Kimi Delta Attention mechanism, and a 1-million-token context window. It's positioned as an agentic coding and reasoning model, not just a chat assistant, with strong self-reported scores on terminal and software-engineering benchmarks.

slides.title: The Biggest Open-Weight Drop of the Month
slides.body: Moonshot AI published Kimi K3's full weights on July 26, 2026 — a day ahead of its own July 27 target — under the Kimi K3 License, via Hugging Face and GitHub.
bullets: 2.8 trillion total parameters, but only 104 billion activate per token
Built for long-horizon agentic coding: navigating repos, running terminal tools, driving compilers
Full weights available for download and self-hosting, not locked behind an API

slides.title: Frontier Scale Usually Stays Behind an API
slides.body: The largest, most capable models have historically been closed — proprietary weights served only through a paid API, with open releases trailing behind on agentic and coding benchmarks.
bullets: Open-weight models have generally lagged closed frontier labs on multi-step coding and tool-use tasks
Serving a multi-trillion-parameter MoE model efficiently requires inference-engine support most stacks don't have by default
Without open weights, researchers can't inspect, fine-tune, or run the model outside the vendor's own infrastructure

slides.title: A New Attention Mechanism Built for Scale
slides.body: Kimi K3 mixes two attention variants across 93 layers and routes through a sparse mixture of experts, keeping the active compute far below the total parameter count.
bullets: 93 layers: 69 use Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), 24 use Gated MLA, plus 1 dense layer — mixed at roughly 3:1
Attention Residuals (AttnRes) improve token efficiency by about 25% for roughly 2% extra compute, per Moonshot's own report
Stable LatentMoE routes each token through 16 of 896 experts plus 2 shared experts — only 104B of 2.8T parameters fire per token

slides.title: Kimi K3 by the Numbers
What a 1M-Token Context Actually Buys You
slides.body: Moonshot's own benchmark numbers target long-horizon software engineering rather than short Q&A.
bullets: An agent can hold an entire mid-size monorepo in context and navigate it without a separate retrieval step
Reported scores: Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.3, FrontierSWE 81.2, ProgramBench 77.8 (raw pass rate), DeepSWE 67.5, SWE Marathon 42.0
The model is described as orchestrating terminal tools directly — compiler runs, test suites, CAD and chip-design workflows — not just producing code snippets

slides.title: The Catch: Size Is Also the Cost
slides.body: Open weights don't mean easy to run — Kimi K3 is a serious infrastructure commitment.
bullets: Full weights are roughly 1.4TB even at MXFP4 precision — this needs a real multi-GPU cluster just to load
For most developers the practical on-ramp is still the hosted API on platform.kimi.ai, not self-hosting
KDA is a new attention variant — inference engines like vLLM and SGLang need dedicated kernel support before it runs at full efficiency

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Kimi K3 is a 2.8T-parameter MoE model with only 104B active parameters per token, released as full open weights on July 26, 2026
Its Kimi Delta Attention + Attention Residuals combination targets long-context efficiency; Stable LatentMoE keeps active compute low
Self-reported benchmarks emphasize agentic coding and terminal tool use over general chat
Running it yourself means multi-GPU infrastructure for a ~1.4TB weight set — most users will hit it through a hosted API instead

questions.prompt: What is unusual about how Kimi K3 uses its 2.8 trillion parameters?
options: Every parameter activates on every token, like a dense model
Only 104 billion parameters activate per token via mixture-of-experts routing
The parameters are split evenly across 8 identical copies of the model
Parameters are only used during training, not inference
questions.explanation: Kimi K3 is a sparse MoE model: each token routes through 16 of 896 experts plus 2 shared experts, so only 104B of the 2.8T total parameters actually compute for that token.

questions.prompt: According to Moonshot's own report, what does Attention Residuals (AttnRes) do?
options: It removes attention entirely in favor of convolution
It improves token efficiency by about 25% for roughly 2% extra compute
It doubles the context window at no extra cost
It replaces the mixture-of-experts routing mechanism
questions.explanation: AttnRes improves cross-layer information flow, which Moonshot reports as roughly a 25% gain in token efficiency for about 2% additional compute — a small tax for a meaningful efficiency gain.

questions.prompt: What is the biggest practical barrier to running Kimi K3 yourself, rather than through a hosted API?
options: The model refuses to run outside Moonshot's own servers
The license forbids self-hosting entirely
The full weight set is roughly 1.4TB, requiring serious multi-GPU infrastructure just to load
It only works with a proprietary chip Moonshot hasn't released
questions.explanation: Even at MXFP4 precision, a 2.8T-parameter model's weights land around 1.4TB — loading that, let alone serving it at low latency, requires a real multi-GPU cluster, which is why most developers will access it via platform.kimi.ai instead.

posts.title: Molt: NVIDIA's Lean Framework for Agentic RL Training
posts.subtitle: About 9.2K lines of core RL code, one asynchronous training loop, and a strict rule: never train on a token the policy didn't generate.
posts.summary: Molt (arXiv:2607.21653), from NVIDIA-NeMo, is a PyTorch-native RL training framework built around a single asynchronous loop and a compact ~9.2K-line codebase — small enough for a researcher, or an AI coding assistant, to trace the entire algorithm end to end. It supports MoE-native parallelism up to 1T-class models and reports performance statistically comparable to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based stack under a matched, fully asynchronous protocol.

slides.title: A Codebase Small Enough to Hold In Your Head
slides.body: Molt is currently the #1 trending paper on Hugging Face Daily Papers, out of NVIDIA-NeMo.
bullets: arXiv:2607.21653 — 'Molt: A Scalable PyTorch-Native Training Framework for Agentic Reinforcement Learning'
Core RL code is about 9.2K lines — compact enough that a researcher can trace the whole algorithm end to end
Built on Ray (placement/async queues), vLLM (rollout generation), and NVIDIA AutoModel + FSDP2, entirely in PyTorch

slides.title: Every RL Idea Gets Buried in Infrastructure
slides.body: Agentic RL research means constant algorithm churn — but mainstream frameworks make every change expensive.
bullets: New estimators, new pipeline stages, and new rollout schemes are the normal pace of agentic RL research
In mainstream frameworks, each change threads through layers of trainer, distributed backend, and rollout glue
That plumbing cost lands on the researcher at every iteration, slowing the actual science down

slides.title: One Async Loop, Strict Token Consistency
slides.body: Molt collapses rollout and training into a single asynchronous loop with a hard invariant on data provenance.
bullets: The policy never trains on a token it did not itself generate — tokens, policy versions, and model semantics stay consistent throughout
One asynchronous loop trains multimodal and mixture-of-experts policies together, instead of separate synchronized rollout/train phases
Supports MoE-native parallelism (tensor, expert, and context parallelism) and scales to 1T-class MoE models like DeepSeek-V3

slides.title: Code Size Against Other RL Frameworks
slides.body: Molt isn't the smallest option here — OpenRLHF is leaner — but it's the only one in this set that's MoE-native and asynchronous from the ground up.

slides.title: Changing an Algorithm, Concretely
slides.body: Picture a researcher who wants to test a new advantage-normalization scheme.
bullets: In a Megatron-based stack, that change typically touches a trainer class, a distributed sharding path, and a rollout scheduler across separate services
In Molt, it's a change inside one asynchronous training loop, since rollout generation (vLLM) and training share the same consistent object
The same loop is designed to handle multimodal policies and MoE routing without a separate code path for each

slides.title: What Molt Doesn't Claim
slides.body: Compact and legible is the point — not necessarily faster or more feature-complete than mature alternatives.
bullets: The paper reports Molt as statistically comparable to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based stack under a matched, fully asynchronous protocol — not that it outperforms one
A compact, readable codebase trades off some of the low-level tuning knobs a larger, more mature stack (verl, at ~62K LOC) has accumulated over time
It's a research framework released alongside a paper — production RLHF pipelines at API-serving scale are a different engineering bar

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Molt's goal is legibility: a codebase small enough (~9.2K LOC) for a person or an AI assistant to trace the full RL algorithm end to end
It enforces a strict invariant — never train on a token the current policy didn't generate — inside one asynchronous rollout/train loop
It's MoE-native and scales to 1T-class models, reporting performance statistically comparable to a Megatron-based stack, not better
It's aimed at research iteration speed, not at replacing mature production RL stacks outright

questions.prompt: What is Molt's central design goal, according to the paper?
options: To be the smallest possible RL codebase in lines of code
To keep the codebase small and legible enough that a researcher (or an AI assistant) can trace the entire algorithm end to end
To eliminate the need for GPUs during training
To replace vLLM as the standard rollout engine
questions.explanation: Molt is about 9.2K lines — more than OpenRLHF's ~7.2K — so the goal isn't raw minimalism, it's a codebase compact and clean enough to reason about in its entirety.

questions.prompt: What invariant does Molt enforce inside its asynchronous training loop?
options: The policy must never update more than once per hour
The policy never trains on a token it did not itself generate — tokens, policy versions, and model semantics stay consistent
Only text-only policies are permitted, no multimodal training
Training and rollout must run on physically separate clusters
questions.explanation: That consistency guarantee — no training on tokens the current policy didn't produce — is what lets Molt run rollout and training as one asynchronous loop without drifting out of sync.

questions.prompt: How does the paper describe Molt's performance relative to a state-of-the-art Megatron-based stack?
options: Significantly faster in every benchmark tested
Statistically comparable, under a matched fully asynchronous protocol
Slower, but easier to install
The paper does not compare performance at all
questions.explanation: The claim is parity, not superiority: under a matched async protocol, Molt performs statistically comparably to a mature Megatron-based stack — the win is in codebase legibility, not raw throughput.

posts.title: GRPO: Reasoning RL Without a Critic Model
posts.subtitle: Sample a group of answers to the same prompt, score them against each other, and you've replaced PPO's second neural network with arithmetic.
posts.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains reasoning models without PPO's separate critic network. It samples a group of completions per prompt, scores each with a reward function, and normalizes each completion's reward against the group's own mean and standard deviation to get an advantage — cutting memory and compute roughly in half at the cost of needing many rollouts per prompt.

slides.title: The RL Recipe Behind Modern Reasoning Models
slides.body: GRPO was introduced by DeepSeek and became the core RL algorithm behind DeepSeek-R1-style reasoning training.
bullets: Core idea: replace PPO's learned critic (value network) with a group of sampled answers scored against each other
No second neural network to train alongside the policy — roughly half the memory and compute of PPO
Built for tasks with a cheap, checkable reward: a right/wrong math answer, a passing test suite

slides.title: PPO's Critic Is Expensive and Starts Wrong
slides.body: Standard PPO needs a critic the same size as the policy just to estimate partial-response value.
bullets: The critic (value network) is typically the same size as the policy — you're training two large models at once
That critic starts untrained and noisy, and its early errors feed straight into the advantage estimate used to update the policy
For reasoning tasks where the true reward (correct or not) is cheap to compute directly, a learned value estimate is often unnecessary overhead

slides.title: Group Sampling Replaces the Value Function
slides.body: GRPO swaps the critic for a purely statistical baseline computed from the policy's own samples.
bullets: For each prompt, sample a group of G completions (commonly 8-64) from the current policy
Score every completion with the reward function — often a simple, verifiable check
Advantage = (completion's reward − group mean) / group standard deviation — no learned critic required
A KL penalty against a reference policy is added directly in the loss to keep updates from drifting too far

slides.title: PPO vs. GRPO

rows: Per-sequence, broadcast to all its tokens

slides.title: Training on a Single Math Problem
slides.body: A worked, simplified pass through one GRPO update step.
bullets: Prompt: a competition math problem. Sample G=16 completions from the current policy
A rule-based checker scores each: 1 if the final answer matches ground truth, 0 otherwise
Say 5 of 16 get reward 1 — group mean is 0.3125; those 5 get positive advantage, the other 11 get negative advantage
The update pushes the model toward token patterns shared by the 5 correct traces relative to the group average — not toward any fixed external target

slides.title: Where GRPO Struggles
slides.body: The group-relative design has real failure modes, not just savings.
bullets: If every completion in a group gets the same reward (all correct or all wrong), the group standard deviation is zero and every advantage collapses to ~0 — a wasted rollout batch with no learning signal
It needs G rollouts per prompt before a single gradient step, shifting the cost from training compute to inference/rollout compute
It depends on a cheap, reliable, repeatable reward function — it doesn't help much when scoring requires an expensive or noisy judge
Its arithmetic-mean aggregation across a group can be swayed by outlier importance-sampling ratios during off-policy updates — see the GMPO post on this feed, which patches exactly this

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: GRPO replaces PPO's learned critic with a group-relative statistical baseline: advantage = (reward − group mean) / group std
This drops a full second neural network from training, at the cost of needing many rollouts (G completions) per prompt
It works best with cheap, verifiable rewards — math answers, passing tests — not open-ended judged tasks
A group where every sample scores identically produces zero learning signal, which is why difficulty curation matters

questions.prompt: What does GRPO replace, compared to PPO?
options: The reward function itself
The learned critic (value network) with a group-relative statistical baseline
The policy model with a smaller distilled version
The KL penalty against the reference policy
questions.explanation: GRPO drops PPO's separate critic network entirely, replacing its value estimate with a baseline computed from a group of the policy's own sampled completions.

questions.prompt: How is a completion's advantage computed in GRPO?
options: (completion's reward − group mean) / group standard deviation, using rewards from other sampled completions to the same prompt
By asking a separate critic network to predict the value of each token
By comparing the completion only to the single best completion in the group
Advantage is fixed at 1.0 for every completion regardless of reward
questions.explanation: GRPO normalizes each sampled completion's reward against the mean and standard deviation of its own group, producing a per-completion advantage with no learned value function.

questions.prompt: What happens if every completion in a sampled group receives the same reward?
options: Training speeds up because all samples agree
The group standard deviation is zero, so advantage collapses to ~0 for the whole group — no learning signal from that batch
The reward function is automatically retrained
GRPO falls back to using a critic network for that batch only
questions.explanation: With zero variance in the group's rewards, the normalized advantage is ~0 for every completion — the rollouts were computed but produce no gradient signal, which is why prompt difficulty curation matters for GRPO training.

posts.title: Multi-Head Latent Attention: Shrinking the KV Cache Without Shrinking Quality
posts.subtitle: DeepSeek's trick to cache one compressed vector instead of every head's key and value
posts.summary: Multi-Head Latent Attention compresses every token's keys and values into one small low-rank latent vector instead of caching them per-head, cutting KV-cache memory far more than GQA while keeping a separate small slice for RoPE. A 'weight absorption' trick at inference means the model never has to reconstruct full-size keys, so the savings are real, not just a compress-then-decompress illusion.

slides.title: One Vector to Cache Them All
slides.body: Every token an LLM generates forces it to store a key and value vector per attention head, per layer, for the rest of the conversation. Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) — the mechanism behind DeepSeek-V2/V3 — replaces that whole per-head cache with one small compressed vector per token.

slides.title: The KV Cache Is the Real Memory Bottleneck
slides.body: Model weights are a fixed cost. The KV cache is not — it grows with every token in context, across every request you're serving concurrently.
bullets: Standard multi-head attention (MHA) caches a separate K and V vector per head per layer: total size scales with n_heads × d_head × n_layers × sequence_length.
At 128K context with dozens of layers and heads, the KV cache per request can rival or exceed the size of the model's own activations in flight.
Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) cut this by sharing K/V across heads — but they throw away per-head expressiveness to do it, trading some quality for memory.
The real question MLA asks: can you shrink the cache without sharing away information, by compressing it instead?

slides.title: Compress K and V Into One Latent Vector
slides.body: Instead of projecting each token into n_heads separate key/value pairs and caching all of them, MLA first projects the token down into a single low-rank latent vector, then expands back up to per-head keys and values only when needed.
bullets: A down-projection matrix maps the token's hidden state to a compressed latent c (e.g. a few hundred dimensions) — this is the only thing that gets cached per token.
Separate up-projection matrices reconstruct the full per-head K and per-head V from that same latent c on demand.
Because c is shared across all heads, the cache no longer scales with n_heads at all — only with the latent dimension, which is far smaller than n_heads × d_head.
Unlike GQA's sharing, no information about individual heads is discarded ahead of time — it's recoverable from c, just compressed.

slides.title: Why RoPE Needs Its Own Lane
slides.body: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) works by rotating query/key vectors by an angle proportional to position — but rotation doesn't commute cleanly with the low-rank compression MLA relies on.
bullets: If you compress a token's content into c and then try to apply a position-dependent rotation afterward, the relative-position math RoPE depends on breaks down.

MLA's fix: split each key into two parts — a compressed 'content' key (from the shared latent c) and a small separate 'decoupled RoPE' key computed directly per head, carrying only positional information.
The decoupled RoPE slice is small (a few dozen dimensions) and IS cached per-token, alongside the compressed latent — so the total cache is latent + small RoPE slice, not zero.
This split is why MLA isn't simply 'GQA with a smaller rank' — it's a structurally different way of separating content from position.

slides.title: The Weight-Absorption Trick Makes the Savings Real
slides.body: Compressing and then decompressing on every attention step would just move the memory problem into extra compute. MLA avoids that by folding the projection matrices together algebraically.
bullets: At inference, the query's up-projection and the key's up-projection are combined ('absorbed') into a single matrix applied directly to the query and the cached latent c.

This means the model never actually materializes full per-head keys during decoding — the score is computed straight from the compressed latent, so only c (plus the small RoPE slice) ever needs to sit in the cache.
The same absorption trick applies to values on the output side, folding the value up-projection into the attention-output projection.

This is the detail that makes MLA a genuine cache-size win rather than a compress-then-expand illusion — but it also means inference kernels have to be written specifically to exploit it (see the pitfalls slide).

slides.title: MLA vs. the Alternatives
slides.body: Each attention variant sits on a different point of the memory-vs-quality tradeoff curve.
bullets: DeepSeek's own reported comparison (DeepSeek-V2 vs. its dense DeepSeek 67B predecessor): about a 93% cut in KV cache size and roughly 5.7x higher max generation throughput, while matching or beating the dense model on benchmarks.
That combination — cache smaller than GQA typically achieves, with no measured quality loss versus full MHA — is the headline claim MLA is built around.

rows: Full K, V for every head
One shared K, V for all heads
K, V shared within small head groups
Small quality drop, moderate cache cut
One compressed latent + small RoPE slice
Matches/beats MHA in DeepSeek's reported results

slides.title: Worked Example: Serving Long-Context Requests
slides.body: Picture a 64-layer model with 128 attention heads of dimension 128, serving requests at a 128K-token context length.
bullets: Full MHA cache per token across all layers: 64 layers × 128 heads × 128 dims × 2 (K and V) = over 2 million values per token — at 128K context, that's the dominant cost of serving even a single long request.
GQA with, say, 8 shared groups cuts that by roughly 16x versus full MHA — a real win, but the cache still scales with sequence length × groups × head_dim.
MLA replaces the per-head total with one shared latent (e.g. ~512 dims) plus a small RoPE slice (e.g. ~64 dims) per token — independent of how many heads the model has.

The practical payoff: on the same GPU memory budget, a serving system can hold far more concurrent long-context requests in flight, which is exactly what made DeepSeek-V2/V3's low API pricing viable at scale.

slides.title: Where MLA Costs You Something
slides.body: MLA is not a free lunch — it trades implementation complexity for memory, and that trade isn't always worth making.
bullets: It only helps the KV cache (memory during decoding) — prefill compute is still the same attention cost as before; MLA doesn't speed up processing a long prompt for the first time.

The weight-absorption trick requires custom attention kernels (frameworks like vLLM and SGLang needed dedicated MLA kernels) — a naive implementation that decompresses c on every step loses most of the benefit.
The extra architectural pieces (down-projection, two up-projections, decoupled RoPE slice) add real training and debugging complexity versus GQA's simple head-grouping.

For smaller models or short-context workloads where the KV cache was never the bottleneck, GQA's simplicity is usually the better engineering call — MLA earns its complexity at large scale and long context.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: MLA caches one shared compressed latent vector per token instead of per-head keys and values, decoupling cache size from head count entirely.
A separate small RoPE-carrying slice is needed alongside the latent, because rotation and low-rank compression don't commute.
Weight absorption at inference means the model scores attention directly against the compressed latent — full keys are never reconstructed, so the cache savings are real.
It's a scale play: worth the added kernel and training complexity mainly when long context and high concurrency make KV cache the actual bottleneck.

questions.prompt: What does Multi-Head Latent Attention actually store in the KV cache per token?
options: A full key and value vector for every attention head, same as standard MHA
One compressed low-rank latent vector shared across heads, plus a small decoupled RoPE slice
Only the value vectors, discarding keys entirely
A single shared key and value vector for all heads, identical to MQA
questions.explanation: MLA's core idea is compression, not sharing: it caches one small latent vector (reconstructable into per-head K/V via up-projections) plus a tiny separate slice that carries RoPE's positional information. That's structurally different from MQA/GQA, which cache actual shared K/V vectors.

questions.prompt: Why can't RoPE just be applied directly to the compressed latent vector?
options: RoPE only works on value vectors, never on keys
Rotation by a position-dependent angle doesn't commute with the low-rank compression, breaking the relative-position property RoPE relies on
RoPE requires floating point precision that compressed vectors can't provide
It can be applied directly — MLA doesn't actually need a separate RoPE path
questions.explanation: RoPE's relative-position trick depends on applying rotation directly to the vectors used in the dot product. Compressing first (or after) and rotating breaks that algebraic relationship, so MLA carves out a small separate per-head slice computed and rotated independently of the shared compressed content.

questions.prompt: What problem does the 'weight absorption' trick solve at inference time?
options: It compresses the model's weights to reduce disk storage
It lets the model skip computing attention scores entirely for cached tokens
It folds up-projection matrices into the query/output projections so full per-head keys never need to be reconstructed, keeping only the compressed latent in the cache
It removes the need for a separate value projection
questions.explanation: Without absorption, you'd have to decompress the latent back into full per-head keys on every step to compute attention — defeating the memory savings. Folding the projections together lets the model score directly against the compressed latent, so decompression never has to happen explicitly.

posts.title: The Outbox Pattern: Making a DB Write and an Event Publish Atomic
posts.subtitle: How to stop losing (or duplicating) events when a database commit and a broker publish can't share a transaction
posts.summary: Updating a database and publishing an event to a message broker look like one logical action but are really two separate systems with no shared transaction — so a crash between them silently drops or duplicates the event. The transactional outbox pattern fixes this by writing the event into a table in the SAME local database transaction as the business row, then relaying it to the broker asynchronously via a poller or a change-data-capture tool like Debezium. It guarantees at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once, so downstream consumers still need to be idempotent.

slides.title: One Business Action, Two Systems That Must Agree
slides.body: Modern services often need to update a database AND publish an event ('OrderCreated', 'PaymentCaptured') so other services can react. Doing both reliably — without losing the event or duplicating it — is a surprisingly hard distributed-systems problem, and the fix has a name: the Transactional Outbox pattern.

slides.title: The Dual-Write Problem: Two Writes, No Shared Transaction
slides.body: A database and a message broker are separate systems with separate commit protocols — ordinary client libraries can't wrap both in one ACID transaction.
bullets: Commit-then-publish: if the process crashes or the broker call fails between the two steps, the order exists but the event never fires — billing, shipping, and inventory never find out
Publish-then-commit: a consumer can react to an order that the database transaction later rolls back, so downstream systems see something that never really happened

Distributed transactions (XA/2PC) could cover both, but most modern brokers (Kafka, SNS/SQS, most cloud pub/sub) don't support two-phase commit at all, and the 2PC that does exist is slow and fragile across a network partition
This isn't a rare edge case — it fires on every deploy restart, every broker blip, every OOM-kill, at whatever rate those events already occur in production

slides.title: Write the Event to Your Own Database, Not the Broker
slides.body: The outbox pattern turns a two-system atomicity problem into a one-system one: write the business row and the event into the SAME database transaction, then relay the event out asynchronously.
bullets: Add an 'outbox' table (id, event_type, payload, created_at, published) in the same schema as your business tables
One local transaction inserts both the Order row and the matching OutboxEvent row — a single-database transaction is something every relational DB already guarantees atomically

Because the business write and the event write commit or roll back together, it's now impossible to get one without the other — the dual-write race is eliminated at the source, not patched around afterward
A separate relay process (poller or CDC reader) later reads unpublished outbox rows and forwards them to the broker, marking each one published once the broker acknowledges

slides.title: Two Ways to Build the Relay: Poll or Tail the Log
slides.body: Moving rows from the outbox table to the broker can be done two ways, with a real tradeoff between simplicity and latency/load.
bullets: Polling relay: a background job runs a 'WHERE published = false' query every N milliseconds, publishes each row, then flags it — simple to build, but adds polling latency and steady read load on the hot table

CDC relay: a tool like Debezium tails the database's write-ahead log / binlog directly and streams new outbox rows to Kafka the instant they commit — near-zero added latency and no polling load, at the cost of running an extra CDC pipeline
Either relay only ever needs at-least-once delivery, never exactly-once — it can crash and safely redeliver, which keeps the relay's own logic simple
Cleanup matters: outbox rows need a TTL or archival job, or the table grows unbounded — most teams delete or archive rows some fixed time after they're marked published

slides.title: Walking Through an Order Being Placed
slides.body: A concrete trace of the pattern end to end for an e-commerce checkout.
bullets: 1) Checkout service opens one local transaction: insert into 'orders' and insert into 'outbox' (event_type='OrderCreated') — both commit together, or neither does
2) Checkout service returns '201 Created' to the customer immediately — it never waited on the broker, so a Kafka outage can't block checkout
3) A Debezium connector notices the new outbox row in the binlog within milliseconds and publishes an 'OrderCreated' event onto the 'orders' Kafka topic
4) Billing and Inventory each consume that event independently and record the order_id in their own dedup table, so if the event is ever redelivered, the second delivery is a safe no-op

slides.title: Outbox vs. the Alternatives
slides.body: The other options either fail under failure or cost far more to operate.

rows: None — a crash between the two calls silently drops or duplicates the event
Strong, only if every participant supports 2PC
High — most brokers don't support it; adds coordinator latency and blocks under partition
Strong — one local DB transaction covers both writes
Low — one extra table, one background job
Medium — requires operating a CDC/Kafka Connect pipeline

slides.title: What the Pattern Doesn't Solve For You
slides.body: Outbox fixes the dual-write race, not every downstream ordering or delivery concern — those still need explicit design.
bullets: Delivery is at-least-once, never exactly-once — every consumer MUST be idempotent (dedupe by event id or order id), or a redelivered event double-charges a customer or double-decrements inventory
Ordering is only guaranteed per partition key, not globally — partition Kafka by aggregate id (e.g., order_id) if a consumer needs to see 'OrderCreated' before 'OrderShipped' for the same order
It adds a small write to the local transaction (one more insert) and a small end-to-end delay between commit and downstream visibility — typically milliseconds with CDC, seconds with a naive poller
Skip it for a genuinely single-service feature with no external consumers — the pattern earns its complexity only once another service or system needs to react to your write

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: The transactional outbox pattern turns a two-system atomicity problem you can't solve into a one-system atomicity problem your database already solves.
bullets: The same local transaction writes the business row and the event row — the database's own ACID guarantee is what makes the pattern work
A relay (poller or CDC like Debezium) asynchronously moves outbox rows to the broker, retrying freely since delivery is at-least-once
Consumers must be idempotent — the pattern relocates the atomicity problem, it doesn't erase the need for dedup logic downstream
Used under the hood by most serious event-driven systems — order pipelines, payment flows, saga orchestrators — wherever a DB write must reliably trigger a downstream event

questions.prompt: In the naive 'commit to the DB, then publish to the broker' approach, what specifically can go wrong?
options: Nothing — it's safe as long as the broker has high availability
If the process crashes or the broker call fails after the DB commit, the event is silently lost even though the business write succeeded
The database transaction automatically rolls back whenever the broker publish fails
The broker automatically polls the database to recover any missed writes
questions.explanation: The DB commit and the broker publish are two independent operations with no shared transaction. A crash or network failure between them loses the event while the business data quietly stays committed — that's the dual-write problem.

questions.prompt: Why does writing the event into an 'outbox' table in the same database solve the dual-write problem?
options: Because outbox tables are replicated automatically to the message broker
Because it turns two separate-system writes into one local ACID transaction, so both commit or neither does
Because outbox tables have no schema, so writes to them are instantaneous
Because the broker reads directly from the outbox table instead of from a topic
questions.explanation: The core trick is reducing two systems to one: the business row and the event row both live in the same database, so the database's existing transactional guarantee makes them atomic together — no distributed transaction protocol required.

questions.prompt: A CDC-based relay (e.g., Debezium) redelivers an 'OrderCreated' event after a consumer restart. What must the consumer do to handle this safely?
options: Reject all events that arrive after any consumer restart
Process the event again unconditionally, since duplicates don't matter
Track processed event or order ids and treat the redelivery as a no-op (idempotent processing)
Configure the outbox table to guarantee exactly-once delivery instead
questions.explanation: Outbox relays only guarantee at-least-once delivery, so redelivery is expected and normal. Consumers must dedupe (e.g., by event id or order id) so a repeated event is a safe no-op rather than a double-charge or double-decrement.

posts.title: RoPE: Encoding Position by Rotating Vectors, Not Adding to Them
posts.subtitle: The trick that lets a dot product 'know' the distance between two tokens
posts.summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) encodes a token's position by rotating its query and key vectors by an angle proportional to that position, instead of adding a position vector to the input. Because rotation matrices compose, the attention dot product between a rotated query and key ends up depending only on their relative distance — giving relative position awareness for free at every layer. It's why LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, PaLM, and GPT-NeoX all use it, and why extending context length usually means rescaling RoPE's rotation frequencies rather than retraining from scratch.

slides.title: What If Position Was a Rotation, Not an Addition?
slides.body: Early transformers (BERT, GPT-2) gave each position its own learned vector and added it to the token embedding. RoPE (Su et al., 2021) does something stranger and more elegant: it rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position, inside every attention layer.

slides.title: Absolute Position Vectors Don't Compose Into Relative Distance
slides.body: Attention should care about how far apart two tokens are, not their raw index in the sequence — 'the word 3 tokens back' should mean the same thing whether it's tokens 5-8 or tokens 500-503.
bullets: Learned absolute position embeddings (GPT-2, BERT) add a fixed per-index vector once, at the input — attention then has to indirectly infer relative distance from the sum, which it does imperfectly
A model trained on 512 or 1024 positions has literally never seen an embedding for position 2000 — there's nothing principled to do at longer lengths

Sinusoidal absolute embeddings (original 'Attention Is All You Need') were designed to let relative position be recovered via a linear function, but in practice models still generalize poorly past their training length
What you actually want: a scheme where the interaction between token m and token n depends mathematically only on (m - n), automatically, in every layer

slides.title: Rotate Q and K by an Angle Proportional to Position
slides.body: RoPE splits each query/key vector into pairs of dimensions and treats each pair as a 2D point, then rotates that point by angle m·θᵢ, where m is the token's position and θᵢ = base^(-2i/d) gives each dimension pair its own rotation frequency (base is typically 10000, exposed in configs as 'rope_theta').
bullets: Low-index dimension pairs (small i) get a large θᵢ and rotate fast, capturing fine-grained local position; high-index pairs rotate slowly, capturing coarse long-range position — one embedding, many frequencies at once
The rotation is applied fresh to Q and K inside every attention layer, not once at the input — so every layer gets direct access to position, not a diluted signal passed up from layer 1

Key algebraic fact: rotation matrices compose, so R(mθ)ᵀ · R(nθ) = R((n-m)θ) — when you dot a rotated query at position m against a rotated key at position n, the absolute positions cancel and only (n-m) survives
No extra parameters, no added vectors, no lookup table — it's a deterministic function of position applied to the same Q/K projections you already compute

slides.title: A Minimal Worked Example
slides.body: Take a toy 4-dimensional query vector split into two 2D pairs. Each pair gets its own frequency, and rotating by position turns 'where am I' into 'how far apart are we' automatically once you take a dot product.
bullets: Pair 1 uses θ₁ = 10000^(0/4) = 1.0 rad/position — rotates a full circle roughly every 6 tokens, encoding fine local offsets
Pair 2 uses θ₂ = 10000^(-2/4) = 0.01 rad/position — takes ~628 tokens per full rotation, encoding coarse long-range position

At position m=50, pair 1 has rotated 50 radians (wrapped many times); at position n=53, the *difference* between the two pairs' rotation is exactly 3θ₁ regardless of whether m,n were 50,53 or 5000,5003
This is exactly what LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen2, PaLM, and GPT-NeoX compute for every one of their (typically 64-128) dimension pairs per head, at every layer

slides.title: Three Ways to Tell Attention Where a Token Is
slides.body: RoPE isn't the only answer — ALiBi skips rotation entirely and just penalizes attention scores by distance.

rows: Add a per-index vector to the input once
Poor — undefined past the max trained index
Rotate Q/K per layer; dot product depends on relative distance
Degrades past training length unless frequencies are rescaled
Add a fixed linear distance-based penalty to attention scores
Strong zero-shot extrapolation, no rescaling needed

slides.title: Extending Context Without Retraining From Scratch
slides.body: A model trained with RoPE at a 4096-token context still breaks down well before 8192 tokens, because the low-frequency dimension pairs never saw rotation angles that large during training — it's out-of-distribution, not a hard limit.
bullets: Position Interpolation (Chen et al., 2023): linearly compress position indices by the scale-up factor so angles stay in the trained range — cheap, but blurs fine-grained local resolution
NTK-aware scaling: instead of compressing positions, increase the base frequency itself so high-frequency (local) pairs keep their resolution while low-frequency pairs stretch to cover the new range
YaRN (2023) combines NTK-aware interpolation with a per-frequency ramp, and was used to stretch LLaMA-family models to 128K context with a comparatively small amount of continued fine-tuning
Code Llama's long-context variant took a blunter route: it raised the RoPE base frequency from 10000 to 1,000,000 and continued pretraining, pushing usable context out to 100K tokens

slides.title: When RoPE Helps — and Where It Bites
slides.body: RoPE is now close to a default choice for decoder-only LLMs, but it's not free of sharp edges.
bullets: Pitfall: RoPE is easy to implement subtly wrong — mixing up the 'rotate half' interleaving convention between training and inference silently corrupts every position past the first few tokens
Pitfall: naive fine-tuning at a longer context without adjusting rope_theta just extrapolates into untrained rotation angles — you'll get degraded, not absent, outputs, which can hide the bug

When NOT to reach for it: for encoder-only bidirectional models or very short fixed-length inputs, the extrapolation problem barely matters, so simpler learned absolute embeddings are fine and cheaper to reason about

RoPE composes cleanly with GQA and KV-caching (it's applied to Q/K before caching, so cached K vectors already carry their rotation) — but that also means changing rope_theta after training invalidates any KV cache computed under the old base

questions.prompt: Where does RoPE apply its rotation?
options: Once, to the token embeddings before the first transformer layer
To the query and key vectors, freshly, inside every attention layer
Only to the final output logits before the softmax
To a separate learned position-embedding table indexed by distance
questions.explanation: RoPE rotates Q and K inside every attention layer rather than once at the input. That's what lets every layer directly read off relative position from the dot product, instead of relying on a diluted signal passed up from layer 1.

questions.prompt: Why does rotating Q and K make attention depend on relative rather than absolute position?
options: Because the rotation angles are learned to memorize each pair's distance
Because rotation matrices compose: R(mθ)ᵀ·R(nθ) = R((n−m)θ), so the dot product only retains (n−m)
Because longer sequences automatically get larger vector norms
Because RoPE discards absolute position information entirely before attention runs
questions.explanation: The composition property of rotation matrices is the whole trick: rotating a query by mθ and a key by nθ makes their dot product a function of (n−m) alone. No relative-position lookup table is needed — it falls out of the math.

questions.prompt: A RoPE-based model trained at a 4096-token context degrades sharply past that length. What's the standard fix that avoids retraining from scratch?
options: Remove positional information from the model entirely
Simply increase the inference batch size
Rescale the rotation frequencies (position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN) and briefly continue pretraining
Switch the model to learned absolute embeddings at inference time
questions.explanation: Because the degradation comes from out-of-distribution rotation angles, the fix is to rescale how those angles map to position — via position interpolation, NTK-aware scaling, or YaRN — then do a short continued-pretraining pass, which is far cheaper than training a new model at the longer length.

posts.title: Grouped-Query Attention: The Middle Ground on KV Cache Size
posts.subtitle: Why Llama 2 70B gives 64 query heads only 8 sets of keys and values
posts.summary: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) sits between multi-head attention (one key/value pair per query head, best quality) and multi-query attention (one shared key/value pair for all query heads, smallest cache). By clustering query heads into groups that each share a single KV head, GQA cuts KV cache size and memory-bandwidth cost by the grouping factor while losing under a point of benchmark quality — which is why Llama 2 70B, Mistral, and most modern open models use it instead of full multi-head attention.

slides.title: Not Every Query Head Needs Its Own Keys and Values
slides.body: Standard multi-head attention gives every attention head its own key and value projections. GQA asks: what if several query heads shared one set of keys and values instead?

slides.title: The KV Cache Scales With Every Head You Add
slides.body: During autoregressive decoding, the model caches a key and value vector per token per head per layer so it doesn't recompute them. That cache is what actually limits how much context and how many concurrent requests a GPU can serve.
bullets: Cache size = 2 (K and V) x num_kv_heads x head_dim x num_layers x tokens x bytes_per_value — linear in the number of KV heads
In classic multi-head attention (MHA), num_kv_heads equals num_query_heads, so a 64-head model caches 64 separate K/V pairs per token per layer
On long contexts or large batch sizes, this cache — not the model weights — becomes the memory bottleneck, and moving it in and out of HBM is what caps decode throughput
Multi-Query Attention (MQA, Shazeer 2019) is the extreme fix: collapse to a single shared KV head for all query heads, but that can measurably hurt quality

slides.title: Cluster Query Heads Into Groups That Share One KV Head
slides.body: GQA (Ainslie et al., Google Research, 2023) generalizes MQA: instead of one shared KV head for everything, split the query heads into G groups, and give each group its own single KV head. G=num_query_heads recovers plain MHA; G=1 recovers MQA.
bullets: Grouping factor = num_query_heads / num_kv_heads — e.g. 64 query heads with 8 KV heads means groups of 8 query heads sharing one K/V pair
Cache size shrinks by exactly that grouping factor versus MHA, since you're storing num_kv_heads worth of K/V instead of num_query_heads worth

You can 'uptrain' an existing MHA checkpoint into a GQA model by mean-pooling each group's original KV heads into one, then continuing pretraining on ~5% of the original compute — no need to train from scratch
Empirically, GQA lands close to MHA quality while matching MQA's decode speed — it's a Pareto improvement over the MHA/MQA extremes, not just a compromise

slides.title: Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B Made Different Grouping Choices
slides.body: Both ship GQA, but the grouping factor — and therefore the cache savings — differs based on how aggressively each team wanted to trade quality for memory.
bullets: Llama 2 70B: 64 query heads, 8 KV heads -> grouping factor 8, an 8x smaller KV cache than full MHA, at under 1% cost on most benchmarks versus the MHA baseline
Mistral 7B: 32 query heads, 8 KV heads (head_dim 128) -> grouping factor 4, a 4x smaller cache, combined with a 4096-token sliding window to cut memory further still
8 KV heads is also a convenient number for 8-way tensor parallelism: each GPU shard owns exactly one KV head, so the cache splits cleanly across devices
Smaller open models often skip GQA entirely (num_kv_heads = num_query_heads) because their KV cache was never the bottleneck at their target context length

slides.title: MHA, GQA, and MQA Trade Cache Size for Quality
slides.body: The grouping factor is the one knob that moves you along this curve.

slides.title: Pitfalls: You're Committing to a Grouping Factor Up Front
slides.body: GQA isn't a free knob you tune after the fact — the choice shapes both training and every future deployment of the model.
bullets: The grouping factor is baked into the architecture at (pre)training time; changing it later means re-uptraining, not a config flag
Too aggressive a grouping factor (too few KV heads) starts to show up as real quality loss, especially on tasks sensitive to fine-grained retrieval within long context
GQA reduces memory-bandwidth cost, not compute — the query-side matmuls are unchanged, so it mainly helps memory-bound decode, not compute-bound prefill
When NOT to bother: short-context, low-concurrency deployments where the KV cache was never close to the memory ceiling gain little from GQA and can keep plain MHA's slightly better quality

slides.title: GQA Is Why Modern Open Models Serve Long Context Affordably
slides.body: It's a small architectural change with an outsized effect on serving cost.
bullets: GQA interpolates between MHA (best quality, biggest cache) and MQA (smallest cache, quality risk) by giving groups of query heads one shared KV head each
Cache size drops by exactly the grouping factor — Llama 2 70B's 8x reduction is why it can serve much longer contexts per GPU than an equivalent MHA model
You can retrofit GQA onto an existing MHA checkpoint via mean-pooling KV heads plus a short uptraining run, instead of training from scratch
It composes with other cache tricks — PagedAttention and quantized KV caches both still apply on top of GQA's already-smaller cache

questions.prompt: What does Grouped-Query Attention actually change compared to standard multi-head attention?
options: It removes the KV cache entirely
It clusters query heads into groups that each share one key/value head, instead of every query head having its own
It increases the number of key/value heads beyond the number of query heads
It replaces attention with a convolution
questions.explanation: GQA keeps the number of query heads the same but reduces the number of distinct KV heads, grouping several query heads onto one shared key/value pair — shrinking the cache without touching the query-side computation.

questions.prompt: Llama 2 70B uses 64 query heads and 8 KV heads. Roughly how much smaller is its KV cache than an equivalent full multi-head attention model?
options: About 2x smaller
About 8x smaller
About 64x smaller
The same size — GQA doesn't affect cache size
questions.explanation: The cache shrinks by the grouping factor, which is num_query_heads / num_kv_heads = 64 / 8 = 8. Cache size scales with the number of KV heads, not query heads, so going from 64 KV heads (MHA) to 8 (GQA) is an 8x reduction.

questions.prompt: Why might a team choose plain multi-head attention (MHA) over GQA for a given model?
options: MHA is always faster to train
GQA cannot be implemented on GPUs
If the deployment is short-context and low-concurrency, the KV cache was never the bottleneck, so MHA's slightly better quality can be worth keeping
MHA uses less GPU memory than GQA
questions.explanation: GQA trades a small amount of quality for a smaller, cheaper-to-serve KV cache. If your deployment never gets close to the memory ceiling that cache size would cause, that trade isn't worth making — MHA's full quality comes for free in that regime.

posts.title: Quantization: Fewer Bits Per Weight, Almost the Same Model
posts.subtitle: How LLMs shrink 4x in memory without losing their minds
posts.summary: Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits (int8 or int4 instead of fp16) to cut memory and speed up inference, at the cost of some precision. Naive rounding breaks on the small number of outlier activation channels every LLM has, so real methods like LLM.int8(), GPTQ, and AWQ either isolate outliers or compensate for the error layer-by-layer. The payoff: a 7B model that needs 14GB in fp16 fits in roughly 3.5GB at int4, often with only a small, measurable quality cost.

slides.title: Every Weight Is a Number. Quantization Asks: How Few Bits Does It Need?
slides.body: Models are trained in 16 or 32-bit floating point. Quantization stores the same weights in 8 or even 4 bits, shrinking memory and speeding up matrix multiplies — the technique behind every model you've run on a laptop or phone.

slides.title: fp16 Weights Are the Single Biggest Cost of Serving an LLM
slides.body: Every parameter in fp16 costs 2 bytes, before you even add the KV cache or activation memory needed at inference time.
bullets: A 7B-parameter model in fp16 is ~14GB of weights alone — already close to a single consumer GPU's VRAM
A 70B model is ~140GB, requiring multiple datacenter GPUs just to hold the weights
Bigger weights also mean slower inference: on memory-bound decode steps, moving weights from HBM to compute is the bottleneck, not the math
Halving or quartering the bytes per weight directly cuts both memory footprint and memory-bandwidth-bound latency

slides.title: Round Weights to a Grid, But Handle the Outliers Separately
slides.body: Naive quantization picks a scale factor and rounds every weight to the nearest representable value. It fails on LLMs because a small number of activation dimensions carry enormous, systematic outlier magnitudes that blow up the rounding error for the whole tensor.
bullets: LLM.int8() splits out the ~0.1% of outlier feature dimensions to run in fp16, quantizing everything else to int8 — a mixed-precision decomposition, not uniform rounding

GPTQ quantizes one column of a weight matrix at a time and immediately updates the remaining unquantized columns to compensate for the rounding error just introduced (an approximate second-order correction)
AWQ observes that a small fraction of weight channels matter disproportionately (based on activation magnitude) and protects just those via per-channel scaling before quantizing the rest to 4-bit
All three are post-training methods: no retraining needed, just a small calibration set to measure activation statistics

slides.title: Fitting a 7B Chat Model on a 24GB Consumer GPU
slides.body: The arithmetic is just bytes-per-parameter times parameter count — no benchmark needed to see why this matters.
bullets: fp16: 7B params x 2 bytes = ~14GB of weights, leaving little of a 24GB card for KV cache or batch size
int8: 7B params x 1 byte = ~7GB of weights — frees up ~7GB for a much larger context window
int4 (GPTQ/AWQ): 7B params x 0.5 byte = ~3.5GB of weights — now the same card can serve several concurrent long-context sessions
This is why nearly every locally-runnable open-weight model ships with GPTQ or AWQ quantized variants alongside the original fp16 release

slides.title: Memory Scales Linearly With Bits Per Parameter
slides.body: Bytes-per-parameter is exact arithmetic; quality impact is a general trend, not a fixed number, since it depends on the model and calibration data.

slides.title: Pitfalls: Calibration Data, Kernel Support, and the Sub-4-Bit Cliff
slides.body: Quantization isn't a free lunch — it shifts costs from memory to engineering effort and calibration risk.
bullets: Calibration data must resemble the deployment distribution — quantizing on the wrong domain's text skews which channels get protected and can silently hurt quality on your actual traffic
Speedups aren't automatic: you need kernels that natively compute in low-bit formats (e.g. int4 matmul kernels); without them you pay a dequantize-then-multiply tax that can erase the gain
Quality degradation is non-linear — int8 is often nearly free, but going below 4-bit without quantization-aware training tends to degrade quality sharply, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks

When NOT to use: if you're about to do heavy further fine-tuning on a very different domain, quantizing first can make training less stable — consider QLoRA-style quantized fine-tuning instead of plain PTQ then fine-tune

slides.title: Fewer Bits, Same Model, Different Tradeoff Curve
slides.body: Quantization trades a small, controllable amount of precision for large, predictable gains in memory and often latency.
bullets: int8 quantization is close to a free lunch for most LLMs — use it as the default when memory is tight
int4 (GPTQ/AWQ) roughly quarters memory versus fp16 but requires good calibration data and hardware kernel support to pay off
The core engineering problem isn't rounding — it's handling the small number of outlier weights/activations that naive rounding destroys
Below 4 bits, expect real quality loss unless you invest in quantization-aware training

questions.prompt: Why does naive uniform int8 quantization often degrade LLMs more than you'd expect from just 'losing a few bits'?
options: int8 arithmetic isn't supported on GPUs
A small number of outlier activation/weight dimensions have unusually large magnitudes that a single uniform scale factor can't represent well
int8 requires retraining the entire model from scratch
LLMs don't use matrix multiplication internally
questions.explanation: LLMs have a small number of systematic outlier dimensions with much larger magnitude than the rest. A single scale factor sized to cover those outliers wastes precision on every normal-sized weight, which is why methods like LLM.int8() isolate outliers into a separate fp16 path instead of quantizing everything uniformly.

questions.prompt: What is the key idea behind AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization)?
options: It retrains the model from scratch at 4-bit precision
It quantizes activations but leaves all weights in fp16
It identifies the small set of weight channels that matter most (based on activation magnitude) and protects them with per-channel scaling before quantizing the rest
It only works on models under 1B parameters
questions.explanation: AWQ doesn't touch every channel equally — it uses activation statistics to find which weight channels are most salient, scales those to reduce their quantization error, and quantizes the remaining majority of weights to low bit-width with much less quality loss than uniform rounding.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much smaller is a model's weight memory at int4 versus fp16, for the same parameter count?
options: About 1.5x smaller
About 2x smaller
About 4x smaller
About 10x smaller
questions.explanation: fp16 uses 2 bytes per parameter; int4 uses 0.5 bytes per parameter. 2 / 0.5 = 4x, so a 7B model shrinks from ~14GB to ~3.5GB of weights — pure arithmetic on bytes-per-parameter, independent of the specific quantization method used.

posts.title: LoRA: Fine-Tune a Billion Params by Training a Few Million
posts.subtitle: Freeze the model, learn a low-rank patch instead of the whole matrix
posts.summary: LoRA freezes a pretrained model's weights and learns a small low-rank update (two skinny matrices, B and A) for the attention projections instead of touching every parameter. It cuts trainable parameters and optimizer memory by orders of magnitude, adds zero inference latency once merged, and is the reason task-specific adapters can be swapped in and out of one base model.

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning Trains Every Weight. LoRA Trains a Detour Around It.
slides.body: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes the pretrained weight matrix and learns a small additive update instead — the idea behind almost every 'adapter' or 'LoRA file' you've seen for LLMs and diffusion models.

slides.title: Full Fine-Tuning Means Storing a Second Copy of Everything
slides.body: To fine-tune a model you don't just need its weights in memory — Adam-style optimizers keep two extra moment buffers per parameter, and gradients need a third copy.
bullets: A 7B-parameter model at fp16 is ~14GB of weights alone
Adam's first/second moment buffers (fp32) add roughly 4x the parameter count in extra memory
Result: full fine-tuning a 7B model commonly needs 60-80GB+ of GPU memory, well past a single consumer GPU
Ship 10 fine-tuned variants and you store 10 full model copies on disk

slides.title: Freeze W, Learn ΔW = B·A Where B and A Are Skinny
slides.body: For a frozen weight matrix W (size d×k), LoRA adds an update ΔW = B·A, where B is d×r and A is r×k, and the rank r is tiny — usually 4 to 64 — compared to d and k, which run into the thousands.
bullets: Only B and A are trained; W never changes during training
A is initialized random-Gaussian, B is initialized to zero, so training starts as a true no-op (ΔW = 0)
A learned scaling factor alpha/r controls how much the update contributes
Typically applied to the attention projections (Wq and Wv) rather than every layer

slides.title: GPT-3 175B: 10,000x Fewer Trainable Parameters, No Slower at Inference
slides.body: The original LoRA paper (Hu et al., 2021) fine-tuned GPT-3 175B by only training rank-4 LoRA matrices on Wq and Wv, while matching or beating full fine-tuning quality on several benchmarks.
bullets: Reported ~10,000x fewer trainable parameters versus full fine-tuning GPT-3
Reported ~3x lower GPU memory requirement during training
At inference, B·A is simply added into W once (W' = W + B·A) — zero extra latency, unlike adapter layers inserted in the forward pass
Swapping tasks means swapping a few MB of B/A matrices, not reloading a 175B-parameter model

slides.title: LoRA vs QLoRA vs Full Fine-Tuning vs Prefix Tuning
slides.body: Rank r and which layers get adapters are the main knobs — QLoRA adds 4-bit quantization of the frozen base model on top of the same LoRA math to shrink memory further.

rows: Max quality, have the GPUs to spare
Task adapters on a frozen base model
Fine-tune a 65B+ model on a single GPU

slides.title: When a Low-Rank Patch Isn't Enough
slides.body: LoRA assumes the needed weight update lives in a low-rank subspace — true for many style/domain/instruction shifts, but not guaranteed for every task.
bullets: Picking rank too low can underfit large distribution shifts (e.g. teaching a genuinely new language or skill from scratch)
Serving many different LoRA adapters at once behind one base model needs adapter-aware batching, or you lose the throughput benefit
Merging several LoRA adapters into one model can cause interference between the tasks they were trained for
LoRA can't reduce the base model's inference cost — it only shrinks training cost; the frozen weights still have to run

slides.title: The Core Trick: Approximate the Weight Update, Not the Weight
slides.body: LoRA doesn't shrink the model — it shrinks what has to be learned, by betting that a fine-tuning update is low-rank.
bullets: Freeze the pretrained matrix W; train a low-rank ΔW = B·A instead
Rank r (commonly 4-64) trades adapter capacity for trainable-parameter count
Merge B·A into W after training for zero added inference latency
QLoRA stacks 4-bit base-model quantization on the same idea to fine-tune huge models on one GPU

questions.prompt: In LoRA, what actually gets trained?
options: Every weight in the original matrix W
Two small matrices B and A whose product approximates a weight update
Only the model's bias terms
A separate full-size copy of W
questions.explanation: LoRA freezes W entirely and trains B (d×r) and A (r×k) so that ΔW = B·A approximates the needed update — that's where nearly all the parameter savings come from.

questions.prompt: Why does LoRA add zero extra latency at inference time, unlike inserting adapter layers into the forward pass?
options: It doesn't — LoRA models are always slower to run
B·A can be merged directly into W (W' = W + B·A) before serving, so inference runs through one matrix like the original model
LoRA deletes the original weights entirely
Inference always uses B and A separately, in parallel with W
questions.explanation: Because the update is additive and linear, B·A can be folded into W once training is done — the served model looks exactly like the base model architecture, just with updated weights.

questions.prompt: What does QLoRA add on top of standard LoRA?
options: A larger rank r by default
4-bit quantization of the frozen base model, so a much bigger model fits on one GPU during fine-tuning
Removing the low-rank assumption entirely
Training the full weight matrix instead of B and A
questions.explanation: QLoRA keeps the base model frozen in 4-bit precision while still training LoRA's B/A matrices in higher precision, cutting memory enough to fine-tune 65B+ models on a single consumer-class GPU.

posts.title: Mage-Flow: A 4B Model That Beats 20B-32B Rivals
posts.subtitle: Microsoft's compact image generation-and-editing stack trades brute-force scale for codec-aligned efficiency.
posts.summary: Microsoft's Mage-Flow is a 4B-parameter model for text-to-image generation and instruction-based editing that claims to match 20B-32B rivals like Qwen-Image and FLUX.2. The gains come from re-engineering the tokenizer and training pipeline for efficiency — not from adding parameters.

slides.title: Small Model, Big Claims
bullets: Mage-Flow is a 4B-parameter image generation + editing model from Microsoft Research
Positioned as competitive with Qwen-Image (20B), FLUX.2 (32B), and FireRed-Image-Edit (20B) — models 5-8x larger
The gains come from re-engineering the tokenizer and training pipeline, not scaling parameters

slides.title: Native-Resolution Generation Is Expensive
slides.body: High-fidelity image models typically pay for quality with either huge parameter counts or heavy tokenizers that burn compute before generation even starts.
bullets: Standard VAE tokenizers spend significant compute just encoding/decoding pixels to latents, before any generation happens
Supporting flexible resolutions and extreme aspect ratios (like 4:1 banners) usually means retraining or degraded quality
Scaling to 20B+ parameters is one way to buy quality — but it multiplies serving cost and latency

slides.title: Mage-VAE: An Order of Magnitude Leaner Tokenizer
bullets: Mage-VAE uses one-step diffusion-style encoding/decoding with anchor-latent regularization
Claimed ~12x fewer encode MACs and ~22x fewer decode MACs per pixel than the FLUX.2 VAE, while preserving reconstruction quality
Paired with a Native-Resolution Multimodal Diffusion Transformer trained via rectified flow matching
Native-resolution packing + fused CUDA kernels cut per-step training time from ~1.93s to ~0.78s — about 2.5x faster

slides.title: Punching Above Its Weight Class
Turbo Mode: A Sub-Second Edit
bullets: Mage-Flow ships three variants: Base (30 diffusion steps), RL-aligned (20 steps), and Turbo (4 steps)
On a single A100 at 1024² resolution, Mage-Flow-Turbo generates an image in 0.59s and edits one in 1.02s
It supports resolutions from 512 to 2048px at any aspect ratio, including extreme 4:1 banners — the kind of shape that breaks fixed-resolution models
A designer requesting an instruction-based crop-and-relight edit on a 2048x512 banner gets a result in about a second, not a multi-second round trip

slides.title: What's Still Missing
bullets: Turbo's 4-step shortcut trades some quality for speed — Base (30 steps) is the quality ceiling, Turbo the latency-sensitive option
The size/capability comparisons are the vendor's own framing; independent head-to-head evals against Qwen-Image/FLUX.2 aren't out yet
Mage-VL, the vision-language (understanding) half of the Mage family, is listed as 'coming soon' — this release covers generation and editing only
The efficiency claims are pixel/MAC-level engineering wins, not a new generative capability — don't expect new content types, just cheaper compute for existing ones

slides.title: The Core Idea, Compressed
bullets: Mage-Flow shows efficiency gains can come from re-engineering the tokenizer and training loop, not just adding parameters
A leaner VAE (fewer MACs/pixel) plus native-resolution training let a 4B model target the same use cases as 20-32B systems
Three speed/quality variants (Base/RL/Turbo) let you trade diffusion steps for latency depending on the use case
Mage-VL (understanding) is still pending — for now this is a generation-and-editing story only

questions.prompt: What does Mage-VAE primarily optimize?
options: The diffusion transformer's attention mechanism
Encode/decode compute cost of the tokenizer (VAE)
The text encoder's vocabulary size
The model's total parameter count directly
questions.explanation: Mage-VAE targets the tokenizer, not the diffusion backbone — one-step diffusion-style encoding/decoding with anchor-latent regularization cuts encode/decode MACs per pixel by roughly 12x/22x versus the FLUX.2 VAE.

questions.prompt: Why can a 4B-parameter Mage-Flow target the same use cases as 20-32B models?
options: It uses far more training data than the larger models
It only generates low-resolution images
Claimed efficiency gains come from the tokenizer and training pipeline, not scale
It skips the diffusion process entirely
questions.explanation: The paper's central claim is that a leaner VAE and native-resolution training with fused kernels can substitute for raw parameter count — not that the model is doing less work overall.

questions.prompt: What's the tradeoff between Mage-Flow's Base and Turbo variants?
options: Base only does editing, Turbo only does generation
Turbo uses fewer diffusion steps (4 vs 30) for speed, at some cost to quality
Base runs on CPU, Turbo requires a GPU cluster
There is no difference — they produce identical output
questions.explanation: Base runs 30 diffusion steps for maximum quality, RL-aligned uses 20, and Turbo compresses to just 4 steps — trading some quality for 0.59s/image, 1.02s/edit speed on a single A100.
